set.detail: On 24-25 January 41, in the confusion after Caligula's murder, a praetorian named Gratus found the dead emperor's uncle Tiberius Claudius Germanicus, then fifty and long regarded as unfit for public life because of his limp, tremor and stammer, hiding behind a curtain in the palace. The soldiers carried him in a litter to the Castra Praetoria, where he spent the night. Meanwhile the consuls convened the Senate on the Capitol with the urban cohorts and debated restoring the Republic or electing a new emperor from among themselves. Herod Agrippa I, an old friend of Claudius, acted as go-between, encouraging Claudius to stand firm and advising the Senate to negotiate (Josephus). By the next day the urban cohorts had gone over to the praetorians and the Senate, abandoned, had to confer the powers of the Principate on Claudius. He promised each praetorian 15,000 sesterces, the first explicit donative paid for an accession, a precedent that Suetonius says made him the first emperor to buy the soldiers' loyalty. Coins of 41-42 show the praetorian camp with the legend IMPER RECEPT (the emperor received) and a praetorian clasping hands with Claudius (PRAETOR RECEPT). Claudius declared an amnesty for the senators, executed Cassius Chaerea and a few others for the murder, and recalled exiles, including his nieces Agrippina and Julia Livilla. His lack of senatorial support and his reliance on the army and on his freedmen (Narcissus, Pallas, Callistus, Polybius) shaped his whole reign, which saw the revolt of Scribonianus in 42 and recurrent conspiracies; Seneca's Apocolocyntosis claims that 35 senators and some 300 knights were executed. Modern historians (Levick, Osgood) suggest that the "accident" of his elevation may have been less spontaneous than the sources claim, with Claudius and his supporters among the praetorian officers acting quickly to secure the outcome. His scholarly background as a historian of the Etruscans and Carthaginians and his antiquarian interests left a strong mark on his policies.
set.debate: Whether Claudius's accession was a chance event or a planned coup by his supporters in the guard.

set.detail: In spring 43 Claudius launched the conquest of Britain that Caesar had begun and Caligula had abandoned. The pretext was an appeal from Verica, king of the Atrebates, driven out by the sons of Cunobelinus of the Catuvellauni, Togodumnus and Caratacus, whose expanding kingdom dominated the south-east. Claudius also needed military prestige to secure his position after the revolt of Scribonianus. Aulus Plautius, legate of Pannonia, commanded four legions, II Augusta (under the future emperor Vespasian), IX Hispana, XIV Gemina and XX Valeria, with a similar number of auxiliaries, some 40,000 men in all. The troops at Gesoriacum (Boulogne) at first refused to embark for "beyond the Ocean" until Claudius's freedman Narcissus addressed them from the tribunal and was mocked with cries of "Io Saturnalia", after which they sailed in three divisions. The landing place is debated: Richborough (Rutupiae), where a Claudian ditch system and later monumental arch have been excavated, is traditional, while some scholars argue for a landing near Chichester in Atrebatic territory. The Britons avoided battle at first, then fought a two-day battle at a river crossing (generally identified with the Medway), where Batavian auxiliaries swam across in armour and Hosidius Geta won triumphal ornaments. Togodumnus died soon after. Plautius halted at the Thames and summoned Claudius, who came with praetorians and elephants, spent sixteen days in Britain, took Camulodunum, received the surrender of eleven kings and returned to celebrate a triumph in 44. The client kingdoms of Togidubnus in the south and Prasutagus of the Iceni, and the treaty with Cartimandua of the Brigantes, allowed rapid progress; by 47 the frontier ran roughly along the Fosse Way from Exeter to Lincoln. Vespasian, according to Suetonius, fought thirty battles, subdued two peoples and took over twenty oppida, probably including Maiden Castle and Hod Hill. The conquest was costly and slow, requiring four legions for decades, and Appian and Strabo had already argued that Britain was not worth the expense.
set.debate: Landing site (Richborough in Kent or the Chichester area) and the location of the river battle.

set.detail: Claudius died in the early hours of 13 October 54, aged 63, almost certainly poisoned on the orders of his wife Agrippina so that her son Nero, adopted in 50, would succeed before Claudius's own son Britannicus, then nearly fourteen, came of age. The ancient sources agree on poison but differ on details. Tacitus says the poisoner Locusta prepared the dose, the eunuch taster Halotus served it in a dish of mushrooms, Claudius's favourite food, and when he seemed to vomit it, the doctor Xenophon put a feather dipped in quick poison down his throat. Suetonius gives variants, including poisoning at a banquet of priests on the Capitol, and Dio adds Nero's later quip that mushrooms were "the food of the gods" since Claudius became a god by eating them. Josephus mentions the rumour more cautiously. Claudius's other protector, Narcissus, was conveniently away taking a cure in Campania. Agrippina concealed the death until the astrologically favourable hour; at noon the palace doors opened and Burrus presented the sixteen-year-old Nero to the praetorians, who hailed him after he promised a donative, and the Senate followed. Britannicus was kept in the palace. Claudius was deified, Nero delivering a laudation written by Seneca, which, Tacitus says, provoked laughter when it praised the dead emperor's foresight and wisdom. Seneca at the same time wrote the satirical Apocolocyntosis. Modern scholars have sometimes suggested natural causes, since Claudius was elderly and ill, but most accept murder; the timing, after Claudius showed signs of favouring Britannicus and was reported to have said that it was his fate to endure his wives' crimes and then punish them, points to a motive. Agrippina's temple to Divus Claudius on the Caelian was demolished by Nero, though Vespasian later completed it. Claudius's reign, despite the hostility of the senatorial tradition, saw major achievements: the conquest of Britain, the annexation of Mauretania, Thrace, Lycia and Judaea, the harbour at Portus, the Aqua Claudia, the extension of citizenship and the admission of Gallic senators.
set.debate: Murder by Agrippina (all main sources) or natural death of an elderly, ailing man.

set.detail: Nero, born Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus at Antium in December 37, son of Agrippina the Younger and Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus, was adopted by Claudius in 50 as Tiberius Claudius Nero Caesar, given the toga virilis early in 51 with the title princeps iuventutis, and married to Claudius's daughter Octavia in 53. On 13 October 54, when Claudius died, the praetorian prefect Burrus, Agrippina's appointee, presented him to the guard, which hailed him emperor after he promised a donative of 15,000 sesterces each, matching Claudius's; the Senate conferred his powers the same day. Aged sixteen, he was the youngest emperor yet. His accession speech to the Senate, written by Seneca, promised a return to Augustan principles: he would not judge all cases himself, his household would be kept separate from the state, and the Senate would retain its ancient functions. The first years, later called the quinquennium Neronis, were remembered as a period of good government directed by Seneca and Burrus; Trajan reportedly said that no emperor equalled Nero's first five years, though the phrase may refer to his building works. In practice power was disputed between Agrippina and the two advisers. Coins of 54 show Nero and Agrippina face to face, with her name in the place of honour, and she listened to Senate meetings behind a curtain; when she tried to join Nero on the tribunal to receive an Armenian embassy, Seneca directed him to step down to meet her. Her influence declined from 55, when Nero fell in love with the freedwoman Acte, removed Pallas, and poisoned Britannicus at a family dinner after Agrippina threatened to support his claim. The early Neronian period also saw the appointment of Corbulo to the eastern command, Seneca's De Clementia, and measures to restrict expenditure on games by governors. Modern historians (Griffin, Champlin) stress that the young emperor's dependence on advisers masked tensions that erupted after the murder of Agrippina in 59.

In March 59, during the festival of Minerva (Quinquatria) at Baiae, Nero had his mother Agrippina murdered after the failure of an elaborate plot to make her death look like an accident. The freedman Anicetus, commander of the fleet at Misenum, devised a collapsible boat; after a dinner of reconciliation Agrippina embarked for her villa at Bauli, and the canopy loaded with lead fell, killing her companion Crepereius Gallus, while the boat failed to sink properly. Her maid Acerronia, who cried out that she was Agrippina hoping to be rescued, was clubbed to death by the rowers, while Agrippina, injured in the shoulder, swam to safety and was taken to her villa. She sent the freedman Agermus to tell Nero she had survived. Nero, panicking, consulted Seneca and Burrus; Burrus said the praetorians would not kill a daughter of Germanicus, and Anicetus volunteered. Agermus was accused of carrying a dagger to kill Nero, providing a pretext, and Anicetus with naval officers broke into Agrippina's villa. Tacitus reports her last words to the centurion as she offered her womb: "Strike here" (ventrem feri), where she had borne Nero. Nero sent the Senate a letter, drafted by Seneca, claiming she had plotted against him and killed herself on discovery, listing her past crimes. The Senate voted thanksgivings, and only Thrasea Paetus walked out. Agrippina was cremated on a dining couch and given a modest tomb. The sources differ on Nero's motives: his affair with Poppaea Sabina, whom Agrippina opposed, his resentment of her domination, and rumours of incest. Tacitus's account, the most dramatic, is regarded as substantially accurate in outline, though the collapsing boat has been questioned. The murder marks a turning point in Nero's reign: freed from his mother, he gave rein to his artistic ambitions (the Juvenalia of 59 and the Neronia of 60), and his reliance on Seneca and Burrus declined until Burrus died in 62. Suetonius says Nero was haunted by her ghost and the Furies and tried to summon her spirit through magi.

In 60 or 61 the Iceni and Trinovantes under Boudica, having destroyed Camulodunum, Londinium and Verulamium and killed, according to Tacitus, some 70,000 Romans and allies (Dio says 80,000), faced the governor Gaius Suetonius Paullinus in a final battle somewhere in the Midlands. Paullinus had hurried back from his attack on Mona (Anglesey) with the XIV Gemina and detachments of XX Valeria and auxiliaries, around 10,000 men; II Augusta in the south-west failed to join him because its camp prefect Poenius Postumus refused to march, and he later fell on his sword. IX Hispana had already been mauled under Petillius Cerialis. Paullinus chose a narrow defile with a forest behind him and open plain in front, so that his flanks were protected and the Britons, numbering 230,000 in Dio's inflated figure, could attack only on a narrow front. The Britons brought their families in wagons at the rear to watch the victory. Tacitus gives Boudica a speech claiming to fight as a woman of the people avenging her lost liberty, her scourged body and the violation of her daughters, and Paullinus a brief order to keep the ranks, throw javelins, then advance with shields and swords. The legionaries threw their pila, then charged in wedge formation, followed by the auxiliaries and cavalry; the British host was driven back against its own wagons and slaughtered, women and animals included. Tacitus claims 80,000 Britons died against some 400 Romans killed. Boudica took poison (Tacitus) or fell ill and died (Dio). The site is unknown: candidates include Mancetter (Manduessedum) on Watling Street in Warwickshire, High Cross, Church Stowe and sites near Towcester, and the name "Battle of Watling Street" is modern. The victory was followed by a punitive campaign that devastated the territories of the rebels until the procurator Classicianus and Nero's freedman Polyclitus secured a more conciliatory policy. The revolt and its suppression nearly led Nero to consider abandoning Britain (Suetonius, Nero 18).
set.debate: Location (Mancetter, High Cross, Towcester area) and the reliability of the casualty figures.

set.detail: The Great Fire broke out on the night of 18-19 July 64 in shops around the Circus Maximus at the end facing the Palatine and Caelian, where flammable goods were stored, and spread with the wind through the valley and up the hills. It raged for six days, was checked at the foot of the Esquiline by demolishing buildings, then flared again from the estates of Tigellinus in the Aemilian quarter for three more days. Tacitus says that of the fourteen regions only four were untouched, three were razed to the ground and seven left with a few ruined buildings. Destroyed were the ancient temples of Jupiter Stator, Vesta with the penates, the shrine of Servius Tullius to Luna and the house of the Vestals, the Regia, Nero's own Domus Transitoria on the Palatine and countless works of art and libraries. Nero was at Antium and returned to organise relief: he opened the Campus Martius, the buildings of Agrippa and his own gardens to the homeless, built emergency shelters, brought furniture from Ostia and cut the price of grain to three sesterces a modius. Rumour nonetheless spread that he had sung of the fall of Troy on his private stage while the city burned (Tacitus reports it as hearsay; Suetonius and Dio say he did so from the tower of Maecenas or the palace roof) and that his agents had spread the flames to clear land for a new palace. Tacitus says some sources blamed accident and others the emperor. To deflect suspicion Nero blamed the Christians. The rebuilding introduced the first building code: streets were to be broad and straight, buildings limited in height, partly of fireproof Gabine or Alban stone, with porticoes paid for by the emperor, open courtyards and water supply for fire-fighting. Nero used the cleared land in the centre for the Domus Aurea, which provoked lasting resentment, and imposed levies on Italy and the provinces and despoiled temples for funds. The debasement and weight reduction of the coinage in 64 may also be linked to the costs. Modern estimates of damage vary; archaeologists have found burnt layers of 64 across the Palatine and Forum valley.
set.debate: Accident or arson; Nero's responsibility is doubted by most modern historians (he was at Antium, and his own palace burned).

set.detail: Tacitus provides the only detailed account of the first Roman persecution of Christians, in the aftermath of the Great Fire of 64. "To get rid of the rumour", Nero blamed "those whom the crowd called Chrestians, hated for their crimes". Tacitus explains that the name came from Christus, executed by Pontius Pilate under Tiberius, and that the "pernicious superstition", checked for a while, had broken out again not only in Judaea but in Rome, "where all things horrible and shameful flow together". Those who confessed were arrested first, and on their information "a huge multitude" was convicted, not so much of arson as of "hatred of the human race" (odium humani generis). They were mocked in their deaths: covered in animal skins and torn apart by dogs, crucified, or set alight as torches after dark. Nero offered his gardens on the Vatican for the spectacle and mingled with the crowd dressed as a charioteer, so that pity arose for the victims, "as if they were being destroyed not for the public good but for one man's cruelty". Suetonius mentions the punishment of Christians, "a race given to a new and harmful superstition", among Nero's police measures, without connecting it to the fire. 1 Clement (c. 96) alludes to "a great multitude of the elect" who suffered, including women forced to play roles as Dirce and the Danaids, and Christian tradition placed the deaths of Peter and Paul in this persecution. The episode raises several questions. Some scholars (Shaw, 2015) have argued that the link between the fire and the Christians is a later construction, and that the term "Christians" may be anachronistic for 64; most defend Tacitus. The legal basis is also debated: whether there was a specific Neronian law or edict (an "institutum Neronianum" mentioned by Tertullian) banning Christianity, or whether Christians were punished by magistrates' coercive powers. The persecution was confined to Rome but established a precedent that being a Christian was punishable. Revelation's image of the beast and Babylon drunk with the blood of the saints has been read as a reflection of it.
set.debate: Authenticity of the fire link (Shaw) and the legal basis for the persecution.

set.detail: The Jewish revolt broke out in Jerusalem in spring and summer 66 after years of tension under the procurators Albinus and Gessius Florus. At Caesarea, Greeks sacrificed birds at the entrance of a synagogue in a dispute over access, and the Jewish notables who complained to Florus were imprisoned. Florus then took seventeen talents from the Temple treasury "for Caesar's needs"; when Jerusalemites mocked him by passing round a basket for alms, he let his troops loose in the upper city, killing some 3,600 people, including Jews of equestrian rank whom he had scourged and crucified. Agrippa II and Berenice, who stood barefoot before Florus pleading, tried to calm the people; Agrippa's long speech in Josephus (War 2.345-401) lists the peoples Rome had subdued and the legions garrisoning them, a famous survey of imperial power. The crucial step came when Eleazar son of Ananias, captain of the Temple, persuaded the priests to stop the daily sacrifice for the emperor, effectively a declaration of independence. Fighting broke out between the peace party, backed by Agrippa's cavalry, and the rebels, who burned the High Priest's house, the palaces of Agrippa and Berenice and the archives containing debt records. Menahem, son of Judas the Galilean, seized Masada with its armoury, entered Jerusalem as a king and besieged the Roman garrison in Herod's palace; the high priest Ananias was killed, Menahem was then murdered by Eleazar's men, and the Roman cohort surrendered under an oath of safe conduct and was massacred. Violence spread across the region: at Caesarea 20,000 Jews were killed in a single hour according to Josephus, and Jews and Greeks fought in Scythopolis, Ascalon, Ptolemais and Alexandria, where Tiberius Julius Alexander's legions killed 50,000. In the autumn Cestius Gallus, legate of Syria, marched on Jerusalem with legio XII Fulminata and detachments, failed to take the Temple mount and was routed in the pass of Beth Horon, losing 6,000 men and the legion's eagle. That defeat committed Judaea to full-scale war and led Nero to appoint Vespasian.

Nero died on 9 or 11 June 68 at the suburban villa of his freedman Phaon between the Via Salaria and the Via Nomentana, about four miles from Rome, the last of the Julio-Claudians. In March Gaius Julius Vindex, governor of Gallia Lugdunensis, had rebelled, and on 2 April Galba, governor of Hispania Tarraconensis, was proclaimed at Carthago Nova. Although Vindex was defeated by Verginius Rufus at Vesontio in May and killed himself, the Rhine legions offered the throne to Verginius, who refused; Clodius Macer rebelled in Africa, cutting the grain supply. Nero's response wavered between plans to march against the rebels with an army of concubines dressed as Amazons and fantasies of winning the troops back by weeping or retiring to Egypt to make a living as a lyre-player. The praetorian prefect Nymphidius Sabinus induced the guard to desert him by promising a donative in Galba's name, and the Senate declared Nero a public enemy (hostis). Abandoned by his guards and friends, Nero fled at night in disguise with four companions, including his freedmen Phaon, Epaphroditus and Sporus, hearing as he passed the praetorian camp the soldiers cheering Galba. At the villa, hiding in a cellar, he learned that the Senate had condemned him to be executed "in the ancestral fashion", stripped and beaten to death with rods. As horsemen approached he stabbed himself in the throat with the help of Epaphroditus, saying, in Suetonius's famous report, "qualis artifex pereo" ("what an artist dies in me"). A centurion who tried to staunch the wound heard his last words, "Too late. This is loyalty." He was buried in the family tomb of the Domitii on the Pincian by his nurses and Acte. Suetonius says that for years flowers were placed on his tomb, and edicts were issued as if he were alive, while false Neros appeared in the East in 69, c. 80 and c. 88. The date is either 9 June (Jerome and others) or 11 June (reckoning from Dio's length of reign). His death ended the dynasty and opened the civil wars of 68-69.

Titus Flavius Vespasianus, commander against the Jews since 67, was proclaimed emperor at Alexandria on 1 July 69 by the two legions of Egypt at the instance of the prefect Tiberius Julius Alexander, an apostate Jew; his own army in Judaea swore allegiance on 3 July, and the Syrian legions under Gaius Licinius Mucianus by mid-July. 1 July was later counted as his dies imperii. The move had been carefully prepared: after the death of Otho in April and Vitellius's victory, Vespasian, Mucianus and Titus, who had negotiated a reconciliation between the two generals, held meetings at Berytus and on Mount Carmel, where the priest Basilides gave a favourable oracle. Josephus, then a prisoner, claimed to have predicted Vespasian's rise at Jotapata in 67, and Tacitus and Suetonius record a widespread eastern prophecy that rulers would come from Judaea, which Jews applied to a messiah and the Romans to Vespasian. The plan was that Mucianus would march on Italy with a strong force while Vespasian held Egypt and its grain supply, threatening Rome with starvation. In practice the decisive action came from the Danube legions, who declared for Vespasian in August and under Marcus Antonius Primus invaded Italy without waiting for Mucianus, winning the second battle of Bedriacum in October and taking Rome in December. Vespasian's age (sixty), modest Sabine origins, military reputation and two adult sons, Titus and Domitian, made him an acceptable candidate offering dynastic stability after a year of chaos. The coalition behind him, the eastern legions, the Danube armies and client kings such as Agrippa II, Sohaemus of Emesa, Antiochus IV of Commagene and Vologases of Parthia, who offered 40,000 archers, gave him a strong base. Tacitus remarks that the secret of empire was out: an emperor could be made elsewhere than at Rome. Vespasian's stay at Alexandria, where he performed healing miracles, supplied the charisma his origins lacked.

The Lex de imperio Vespasiani is a bronze tablet, found in the Lateran in the fourteenth century and displayed by Cola di Rienzo in 1347 as proof of the sovereign rights of the Roman people, now in the Capitoline Museums. It preserves the final part of the law, or senatus consultum ratified by the people, conferring powers on Vespasian at the end of 69 or start of 70. Eight surviving clauses grant him: the right to make treaties with whomever he wished; to convene the Senate, propose and withdraw motions and pass decrees by relatio or written communication; to have candidates he recommended for office considered extra ordinem; to extend the pomerium; to do whatever he judged to be in the interests of the state, divine and human, public and private, "as was permitted to the deified Augustus, Tiberius and Claudius"; and exemption from laws from which earlier emperors had been released. A sanction clause frees from penalty anyone acting under it, and a retroactive clause validates everything Vespasian had done before the law was passed, from his proclamation on 1 July. The law is the clearest legal statement of imperial powers and has been central to debates about the constitutional nature of the Principate. Some scholars (Brunt) treat it as typical of the comprehensive grants given to every new emperor (Tacitus, Histories 4.3, mentions that the Senate voted Vespasian "all the usual powers"); others see it as unusual, formalising discretionary power (the "discretionary clause") for a new dynasty without Julio-Claudian lineage. The omission of Caligula and Nero from the list of precedents reflects their condemnation. The retroactive clause shows the legal difficulty of an emperor who had seized power by military proclamation. The text's survival in Rome made it a medieval and Renaissance icon of popular sovereignty and the "lex regia", by which jurists such as Ulpian held that the people had transferred their imperium to the emperor.
set.debate: Whether the law was standard for all emperors or exceptional for the Flavians (Brunt versus Levick and others).

set.detail: Titus, left in command when his father went to Alexandria, began the siege of Jerusalem in April 70, shortly before Passover, with four legions (V Macedonica, X Fretensis, XII Fulminata and XV Apollinaris), detachments from Egypt and Syria and allied contingents, perhaps 60,000-70,000 men. The city was defended by three walls on the north and by rival rebel factions: John of Gischala held the Temple, Simon bar Giora the upper and lower city, and the Zealots under Eleazar ben Simon had been absorbed by John during Passover. Their internal war had destroyed food stores, and pilgrims swelled the population. Titus nearly lost his life on reconnaissance. The third wall (of Agrippa I) fell in May, the second wall after fierce fighting, and in June the Romans built a circumvallation wall of 39 stades in three days to starve the city. Josephus, who served as Titus's interpreter and pleaded with the defenders from outside the walls, describes the famine in harrowing detail, including the story of Mary of Bethezuba who ate her child; deserters who swallowed gold coins were cut open by Arab and Syrian auxiliaries. In July the Antonia fortress was taken and the daily sacrifice ceased. On the 10th of the month of Lous (Av), in late August, the Temple was set on fire. Josephus insists Titus wanted to spare it and a soldier threw a firebrand against orders, while Sulpicius Severus, probably drawing on Tacitus, says Titus decided to destroy it to eradicate the Jewish and Christian religions; modern scholars generally favour the latter. Soldiers sacrificed to their standards in the Temple court and hailed Titus imperator. The upper city fell in September. Josephus gives 1.1 million dead and 97,000 captives, figures widely regarded as exaggerated. John surrendered and was imprisoned for life; Simon was captured and executed in the triumph of 71. The city was razed except for three towers of Herod's palace and part of the western wall, and X Fretensis encamped on the ruins. The Temple treasures, including the menorah, were carried in the triumph and housed in the Temple of Peace.
set.debate: Whether Titus ordered the burning of the Temple (Sulpicius Severus) or tried to save it (Josephus).

set.detail: Masada, Herod's palace-fortress on a 400 m high mesa above the Dead Sea, had been held since 66 by the sicarii under Eleazar ben Yair, a descendant of Judas the Galilean, who raided nearby villages such as Ein Gedi, where Josephus says they killed 700 women and children. After the fall of Jerusalem and the reduction of Herodium and Machaerus, the governor Lucius Flavius Silva marched against it with legio X Fretensis and auxiliaries, some 8,000 men, in the winter of 73/74 (the date is debated between 73 and 74). He surrounded the mountain with a circumvallation wall about 4 km long and eight camps, all still visible as the best-preserved Roman siege works anywhere. On the western side, Silva's men built a ramp on a natural spur of the White Promontory (Leuke), topped with a stone platform, up which they hauled a siege tower with a battering ram. When the ram breached the wall, the defenders built an inner wall of timber and earth, which the Romans set on fire. According to Josephus, Eleazar then persuaded the 960 men, women and children to kill themselves rather than face slavery: ten men chosen by lot killed the rest, then one killed the other nine and himself. Two women and five children who had hidden in a cistern survived to tell the story. The Romans found the dead the next morning, on the 15th of Xanthicus, around Passover. Yigael Yadin's excavations of 1963-1965 uncovered Herod's hanging palace, storerooms, a synagogue, ritual baths, scrolls including Ben Sira and the Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice, and a set of eleven ostraca with names, including "ben Yair", which Yadin connected with the lots. Modern scholars debate the historicity of Josephus's account: his speeches are literary, the number of skeletons found was small, and the ramp may have been only partly artificial. In twentieth-century Israel Masada became a national symbol of resistance ("Masada shall not fall again"), and its use as such has itself been studied critically.
set.debate: Date (73 or 74) and the historicity of the mass suicide as told by Josephus.

set.detail: Vesuvius erupted in 79, destroying Pompeii, Herculaneum, Stabiae, Oplontis and the surrounding villas. The traditional date of 24 August comes from the manuscripts of Pliny the Younger's letter to Tacitus (Letters 6.16), but variant readings and archaeological evidence (autumn fruits such as pomegranates and walnuts, braziers in use, wine already fermenting in sealed jars, a coin of Titus with his fifteenth imperatorial acclamation, and in 2018 a charcoal inscription dated 17 October) have led many scholars to prefer 24 October. The eruption began around midday with a Plinian column of pumice and ash rising some 30 km, which the elder Pliny, commander of the fleet at Misenum, observed from across the bay. The ash fell south-east on Pompeii and Stabiae for about eighteen hours, collapsing roofs. During the night and next morning the column collapsed into pyroclastic surges and flows, superheated avalanches of gas and debris, which reached Herculaneum first, killing the hundreds of people who had sheltered in the boat houses on the shore (skeletons excavated since 1981), and later Pompeii, killing those still in the city, whose voids in the ash were cast in plaster by Giuseppe Fiorelli from 1863. Pliny the Elder, who had sailed to rescue friends at Stabiae, died on the beach, probably of a heart attack or asphyxiation. His nephew, who stayed at Misenum, describes in a second letter (6.20) the earthquakes, the darkness and the panic of the crowds. Titus came to Campania, appointed two consular curators to relieve the area and used the estates of victims without heirs for reconstruction. Some 1,150 bodies have been found at Pompeii, but most of its population of perhaps 10,000-12,000 seem to have escaped. Pompeii was rediscovered in 1748 and Herculaneum in 1738, where the Villa of the Papyri has yielded the only surviving ancient library of carbonised scrolls, now being read by imaging and machine learning. The two cities preserve the fullest record of everyday Roman life, from graffiti and election notices to bakeries and brothels.
set.debate: Date: 24 August (manuscript tradition) or 24 October (archaeological evidence and the 2018 charcoal inscription).

set.detail: The Flavian Amphitheatre, begun by Vespasian around 70-72 on the site of the artificial lake of Nero's Golden House, was dedicated by Titus in 80 with games lasting a hundred days, though the topmost storey and possibly the hypogeum were finished by Domitian. An inscription reconstructed from peg holes, read by Géza Alföldy, records that Vespasian built it "ex manubiis", from the spoils of the Jewish war. The elliptical building (188 by 156 m, about 48 m high) had four storeys of travertine faced with Doric, Ionic and Corinthian half-columns and a top storey with pilasters, holding some 50,000 spectators, seated by rank, with senators at the front, women and slaves at the top. Eighty numbered entrances and a sophisticated system of stairs allowed rapid filling and emptying; awnings (velaria) operated by sailors from Misenum shaded the audience. Dio says the inaugural games included 9,000 animals killed, combats of cranes and elephants, women fighting beasts, and a naval battle staged after flooding the arena, probably before the hypogeum was built. Martial's Book of Spectacles celebrates the shows, including the execution of a criminal dressed as Orpheus mauled by a bear and the contest between the gladiators Priscus and Verus, who fought to a standstill and were both freed by Titus. The building became the symbol of Rome's spectacles. Gladiatorial games continued until the early fifth century (Honorius is said to have banned them after the monk Telemachus was killed in 404) and wild beast hunts until 523. Earthquakes in 847 and 1349 and centuries of quarrying stripped the southern side. The name "Colosseum", first attested in the eighth century, derives from the colossal statue of Nero, refashioned as the Sun, that stood nearby. Its use for executions of Christians is uncertain, though it was later consecrated to the martyrs. The building rewarded the people with the land Nero had taken, as Martial put it: "Rome has been restored to herself".

Mons Graupius was the culmination of Agricola's campaigns in Scotland, fought in the late summer of 83 (or 84, depending on the date of his arrival in Britain). After his sixth season, in which the Caledonians attacked the IX legion's camp at night and nearly destroyed it, Agricola advanced north of the Tay with a fleet shadowing the army along the coast. The Caledonian confederacy, more than 30,000 strong according to Tacitus, under Calgacus, took up position on the slopes of a hill. Tacitus gives Calgacus the famous speech against Roman imperialism ("they make a desolation and call it peace") and Agricola a reply urging his men to end the war. Agricola kept his legions in reserve before the camp and placed 8,000 auxiliary infantry, Batavians and Tungrians, in the centre with 3,000 cavalry on the wings. The Britons, with chariots on the plain, held the high ground. The Batavian and Tungrian cohorts closed to sword range, where the Britons' long swords and small shields were ineffective, and pushed uphill. When the Britons tried to outflank the Roman line from the hilltop, Agricola sent four cavalry wings he had held back, which broke them and attacked from the rear. Tacitus reports 10,000 Caledonians killed and only 360 Romans, a lopsided figure; the next day the burned homesteads and silent hills showed the extent of the rout. Agricola then took hostages from the Boresti and sent his fleet round the north of Britain, which reached the Orkneys. The site is unknown: candidates include Bennachie in Aberdeenshire (near the Durno marching camp, which could hold the army), Raedykes, Megray Hill, the Gask Ridge region and Duncrub; the name, misread in Renaissance editions as "Grampius", gave the Grampian mountains their name. Domitian recalled Agricola in 84/85 and soon withdrew troops from Scotland for the Danube, abandoning the legionary fortress at Inchtuthil around 87, which Tacitus resentfully summarised as "Britain was conquered and immediately let go".
set.debate: Site (Bennachie, Raedykes, Megray, others) and date (83 or 84); the figures and speeches reflect Tacitus's artistry.

set.detail: Domitian was stabbed to death in his bedroom on the Palatine on 18 September 96, aged 44, by a conspiracy of palace staff, apparently with the knowledge of both praetorian prefects (Titus Petronius Secundus and Norbanus) and of his wife Domitia Longina. The immediate motive was fear: after the execution of his cousin Flavius Clemens in 95 and the exile of Clemens's wife Flavia Domitilla, and further executions of senators and courtiers, including his secretary Epaphroditus, members of the household believed they were next. Suetonius and Dio report that Domitian, who feared assassination and had lined his colonnades with reflective phengite stone, had been told by astrologers the day and hour of his death; he had executed the astrologer Ascletarion, whose prediction that he would be eaten by dogs was fulfilled when his pyre was overturned by rain. On the day, after asking the hour and being told the danger had passed, he received Stephanus, a steward of Domitilla accused of embezzlement, who had worn a bandage on his arm for days to conceal a dagger and claimed to bring news of a conspiracy. Stephanus stabbed him in the groin; Domitian fought back, trying to gouge his attacker's eyes and reaching for the dagger under his pillow, which had been removed. Other conspirators, Clodianus, a cornicularius, the freedman Maximus, Satur and a gladiator, joined in, inflicting seven wounds; Stephanus was killed in the struggle. The Senate rejoiced, decreed the erasure of his name from inscriptions and the destruction of his statues (damnatio memoriae), and the same day recognised the elderly senator Marcus Cocceius Nerva, who had been approached in advance, as emperor. The army, which loved Domitian for his pay rise, was angry; the praetorians forced Nerva in 97 to hand over the conspirators Petronius and Parthenius for execution. Domitian's nurse Phyllis secretly cremated him and mixed his ashes with those of Julia Titi in the Flavian temple. Pliny and Tacitus present the reign as a terror, but modern historians (Jones, Southern) credit Domitian with efficient administration, frontier consolidation and building.

In October 97 Nerva, aged and childless, adopted Marcus Ulpius Traianus, governor of Upper Germany, announcing the adoption on the Capitol in front of the temple of Jupiter with the words "May it be good, fortunate and happy for the Senate and Roman people and myself: I adopt Marcus Ulpius Nerva Traianus." The adoption was a response to a crisis. In the summer the praetorians, led by the prefect Casperius Aelianus, had besieged the palace, demanding the punishment of Domitian's murderers; Nerva bared his throat to them but was forced to surrender Petronius Secundus and Parthenius, who were killed, and then to thank the soldiers publicly. His authority was broken, and there were rumours of a conspiracy by Calpurnius Crassus and of rivalry with the governor of Syria. By choosing Trajan, a respected general of senatorial family from Italica in Baetica, son of a distinguished Flavian consul, Nerva gained military backing from the powerful Rhine armies. The decision may have been brokered by senators such as Licinius Sura and Julius Frontinus, and the young Hadrian brought congratulations to Trajan from the Danube armies. Trajan received tribunician power and the title Caesar, and when Nerva died on 27 January 98, succeeded without difficulty, staying on the frontier for more than a year before entering Rome. Casperius and the guilty praetorians were summoned to him and executed. Pliny's Panegyricus presents the adoption as the choice of the best man (optimus), and the idea that selection by merit through adoption was superior to dynastic succession became a theme of second-century ideology, voiced in the speech Tacitus gives to Galba in the Histories (1.15-16). The so-called "adoptive emperors" from Nerva to Marcus Aurelius were, however, also linked by kinship and marriage, and adoption was a solution to the lack of sons rather than a principle. Trajan was the first emperor born outside Italy.
set.debate: Whether adoption was a principle of selection by merit or an expedient forced by childlessness and crisis.
